title: Cap. X Arg. III close: reprobating acts are later than final hardness yet prior to it in the order of decree — so reprobation does not follow from foreseen final unbelief but precedes that foresight (John x. 26)
latin: Haec et alia hujusmodi sunt acta reprobandi posteriora, et tamen finali reprobatorum duritia et infidelitate priora: Ergo ex praevisa finali infidelitate hujus aut illius non consequitur reprobatio ejusdem, sed hanc praevisionem potius antecedit: Quod ex illis Christi verbis facile colligitur, Vos non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis, Joann. x. 26.
pass_a: These and other things of this sort are acts of reprobating that are posterior, and yet prior to the final hardness and unbelief of the reprobate: Therefore from the foreseen final unbelief of this one or that the reprobation of the same does not follow, but rather precedes this foresight: Which is easily gathered from those words of Christ, Ye believe not: for ye are not of my sheep, Joann. x. 26.
pass_b: These and the like are acts of reprobating that come later in the life's course, and yet are prior to the reprobates' final hardness and unbelief. So from this or that one's foreseen final unbelief, his reprobation does not follow — rather it precedes that foresight. Christ's words make it easy: "You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep" (John x. 26).

lemmas.gloss: reprobating acts prior to final unbelief foresight
not believing because not of Christ's sheep

title: Cap. X Arg. III close: 'not being a sheep' is antecedent to not believing — Augustine: not of my sheep because predestined to everlasting ruin, not bought for eternal life by his blood
latin: Non esse ovem hisce in verbis consideratur ut antecedaneum ad non credere: At quid aliud est Non esse ovem quam non esse praedestinatum, vel esse a gratia praedestinatorum rejectum, ut explicat Augustinus, Tract. 48. in Evang. Joan. hisce verbis, Quomodo ergo istis dixit, NON ESTIS EX OVIBUS MEIS? Quia videbat eos ad sempiternum interitum praedestinatos, non ad vitam aeternam sui sanguinis pretio comparatos.
pass_a: Not to be a sheep in these words is considered as antecedent unto not believing: But what else is Not to be a sheep than not to be predestined, or to be rejected from the grace of the predestined, as Augustine explains, Tract. 48. in Evang. Joan. in these words, How therefore did he say unto those, YE ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP? Because he saw them predestined unto everlasting destruction, not purchased unto everlasting life by the price of his blood.
pass_b: In these words, not being a sheep is treated as antecedent to not believing. And what else is not being a sheep than not being predestined — or being rejected from the predestined's grace? So Augustine explains (Tract. 48. on John's Gospel): How then did he say to them, "YOU ARE NOT OF MY SHEEP"? Because he saw them predestined to everlasting ruin, not purchased for eternal life by the price of his blood.

lemmas.lemma: Non esse ovem ... antecedaneum ad non credere

lemmas.gloss: not sheep = predestined to ruin, not bought for life

title: Cap. X Arg. IV: if God passed over none except from foresight of sufficient grace finally despised, it would lie in each one's power to be reprobated or not — elect/reprobate difference would first arise from human wills, not diverse divine placita
latin: Si Deus neminem praeteriret aut reprobaret nisi ex praevisione gratiae suae sufficientis finaliter spretæ et contemptae, sive (quod eodem redit) ex praevisione finalis impoenitentiae et infidelitatis, tum situm esset in potestate uniuscujusque, ut pro arbitrio suo reprobetur vel non reprobetur, atque electus vel non-electus esset. Imo omne discrimen electorum et reprobatorum non ex diversis placitis Divinae voluntatis, sed ex diversis actibus humanarum voluntatum primo exoriretur.
pass_a: If God passed over or reprobated no one except from foresight of his sufficient grace finally despised and contemned, or (which comes to the same) from foresight of final impenitence and unbelief, then it would be situated in the power of every one, that according to his own choice he be reprobated or not reprobated, and be elect or non-elect. Nay, every discrimination of the elect and reprobate would first arise not from diverse placita of the Divine will, but from diverse acts of human wills.
pass_b: Suppose God passed over or reprobated no one except from foresight of his sufficient grace finally despised and contemned — or, what comes to the same thing, from foresight of final impenitence and unbelief. Then it would lie in each person's power, at his own choice, whether he be reprobated or not, elect or non-elect. Nay more: the whole difference between elect and reprobate would first spring not from diverse placita of the divine will, but from diverse acts of human wills.

lemmas.gloss: foresight-scheme puts reprobation in each man's power
elect/reprobate split from human acts first

title: Cap. X Arg. IV: whoever has power over the necessary antecedent has power over the consequent — if believing/not believing from free will excited by sufficient grace is the antecedent to election/reprobation, each can choose either
latin: Id inde evincitur, quia in cujus potestate est antecedens necessarium, in ejusdem etiam est consequens, quod ex eodem antecedente infallibiliter dependet: Si igitur credere, et gratiam oblatam amplecti sit antecedens necessarium ad electionem, et non credere, seu gratiam oblatam finaliter respuere sit antecedens ad reprobationem, et utrumque horum ex libero actu humanae voluntatis sufficienti gratia excitatae dependeat, quid apertius quam esse in potestate singulorum ut reprobentur vel non reprobentur, cum inter haec tanquam contradictoria medium assignari nullo modo possit?
pass_a: That is thence evinced, because in whose power the necessary antecedent is, in the same one's also is the consequent, which depends infallibly from the same antecedent: If therefore to believe, and to embrace offered grace, be the necessary antecedent unto election, and not to believe, or finally to refuse offered grace, be the antecedent unto reprobation, and both of these depend from a free act of the human will excited by sufficient grace, what is more open than that it is in the power of singular persons that they be reprobated or not reprobated, since between these as contradictories a middle can by no means be assigned?
pass_b: That is proved thus: whoever has power over the necessary antecedent also has power over the consequent that depends infallibly on it. So if believing and embracing offered grace is the necessary antecedent to election, and not believing — or finally refusing offered grace — is the antecedent to reprobation, and both hang on a free act of the human will excited by sufficient grace, what is plainer than that it lies in each one's power to be reprobated or not? Between those as contradictories no middle can be assigned.

lemmas.gloss: power over antecedent = power over consequent
no middle between reprobate and not

title: Cap. X Arg. IV: open advocates grant the consequence and find no absurdity — Lessius; but Paul refers both reprobation and election to God's antecedent will of mercy and non-mercy by good pleasure
latin: Qui apertius hanc causam agunt, agnoscunt vim consequentiae, sed minime absurdum arbitrantur, complecti (ut illi loquuntur) electionem et reprobationem ex humani arbitrii actibus dependere. Sic philosophatur Lessius Jesuita. Sed quia Apostolus tam reprobationem quam electionem clare et perspicue retulit ad antecedentem Dei voluntatem, miserentis et non miserentis pro suo beneplacito, alii coguntur aliter respondere.
pass_a: They who more openly plead this cause acknowledge the force of the consequence, but by no means judge it absurd to embrace (as they speak) that election and reprobation depend from the acts of human choice. So philosophizes the Jesuit Lessius. But because the Apostle clearly and perspicuously referred both reprobation and election unto the antecedent will of God, having mercy and not having mercy according to his good pleasure, others are compelled to answer otherwise.
pass_b: Those who plead this cause more openly grant the force of the consequence, yet find no absurdity in holding — as they speak — that election and reprobation depend on acts of human choice. So the Jesuit Lessius philosophizes. But because the Apostle clearly and plainly referred both reprobation and election to God's antecedent will — having mercy and not having mercy according to his good pleasure — others are forced to answer otherwise.

lemmas.gloss: Lessius accepts dependence on free-choice acts
Paul refers both to antecedent divine will

title: Cap. X Arg. IV: Vasquez's word-refuge — reprobation-as-destination-to-punishment may be in each one's power; we mean denied preparation of sustaining/raising grace (angels and men), which Vasquez himself says is not in our power
latin: Vasques igitur, In 1. quaest. 23. disp. 95. cap. 9. in vocabulo reprobationis latebram quaerit, atque respondet, Esse in potestate cujusque reprobari aut non reprobari, si sermo sit de reprobatione quae incipit a destinatione ad poenam. Sed nos (uti saepe praemonuimus) per reprobationem non intelligimus destinationem singularis alicujus personae ad poenam, vel praedamnationem ejusdem, sed negatam praeparationem talis gratiae, quae stantem creaturam efficaciter sustentasset, et ad gloriam perduxisset, ut cernitur in causa Angelorum non-electorum; vel quae lapsam creaturam efficaciter erexisset, et ad vitam aeternam perduxisset, ut in causa hominum non-electorum sive reprobatorum cernitur. Atque hac in re habemus confitentem (qui in aliis nobis adversatur) ipsum Jesuitam, cujus verba apponam: Quum Praedestinari sit gratiam illam, quam Deus novit in nobis effectum habituram, nobis praeparari; et non-praedestinari sit gratiam illam nobis non praeparari, et neutrum horum sit in nostra potestate, efficitur ut praedestinari aut non praedestinari non sit in nostra potestate. Quare hac de causa diximus, non esse in nostra potestate reprobari, si reprobatio pro gratiae negatione sumatur. Haec ille. Ibid. pag. 709.
pass_a: Vasquez therefore, In 1. quaest. 23. disp. 95. cap. 9. seeks a lurking-place in the word reprobation, and answers that it is in each one's power to be reprobated or not reprobated, if the discourse be of reprobation which begins from destination unto punishment. But we (as we have often forewarned) by reprobation do not understand the destination of some singular person unto punishment, or the pre-damnation of the same, but the denied preparation of such grace as would have efficaciously sustained a standing creature, and led it unto glory, as is seen in the case of the non-elect Angels; or which would have efficaciously raised a fallen creature, and led it unto everlasting life, as is seen in the case of non-elect or reprobate men. And in this matter we have confessing (who in other things is adverse unto us) the Jesuit himself, whose words I will set down: Since to be Predestined is that that grace which God knew would have effect in us be prepared for us; and not to be predestined is that that grace be not prepared for us, and neither of these is in our power, it is effected that to be predestined or not to be predestined is not in our power. Wherefore for this cause we have said that it is not in our power to be reprobated, if reprobation be taken for the negation of grace. These things he. Ibid. pag. 709.
pass_b: So Vasquez (In 1. quaest. 23. disp. 95. cap. 9) seeks a refuge in the word reprobation, and answers that it is in each one's power to be reprobated or not — if the talk is of reprobation that begins from destination to punishment. But we (as we have often warned) do not mean by reprobation the destination of some singular person to punishment, or his pre-damnation. We mean the denied preparation of such grace as would have efficaciously sustained a standing creature and led it to glory — as in the non-elect angels — or would have efficaciously raised a fallen creature and led it to everlasting life — as in non-elect or reprobate men. And on this point we have the Jesuit himself confessing (though elsewhere he opposes us). His words: Since to be Predestined is that grace which God knew would have effect in us be prepared for us, and not to be predestined is that that grace not be prepared for us, and neither is in our power, it follows that to be predestined or not is not in our power. For that reason we have said it is not in our power to be reprobated, if reprobation is taken for negation of grace (Ibid. pag. 709).

lemmas.gloss: our sense: denied preparation of sustaining/raising grace

title: Cap. X Arg. IV close: their opinion that strips God of election/reprobation liberty under pretext of foreseen faith/unbelief is not true — we say with Paul God does all by counsel of his will (Eph. i. 11)
latin: Non est ergo veritati consentanea illorum opinio, qui electionis et reprobationis libertatem, sub praetextu praevisae fidei et infidelitatis, Deo plane eripiunt; et quod homines in electos et reprobatos dispeccati, id discriminis quoad personas singulares ex antecedaneis et discriminatis hominum actibus contingenter evenisse docent. Nos, si ulla in re, tum praecipue in hac electione et praeteritione, cum Apostolo dicimus, Deum facere omnia ex consilio voluntatis suae, Ephes. i. 11.
pass_a: That opinion therefore of theirs is not agreeable unto truth, who under pretext of foreseen faith and unbelief plainly snatch from God the liberty of election and of reprobation; and teach that what has distributed men into elect and reprobate, that discrimination as to singular persons has contingently come to pass from antecedent and discriminated acts of men. We, if in any matter, then especially in this election and preterition, say with the Apostle that God does all things from the counsel of his will, Ephes. i. 11.
pass_b: So their opinion is not agreeable to truth — those who, under pretext of foreseen faith and unbelief, plainly snatch from God the liberty of election and reprobation, and teach that the discrimination which has sorted men into elect and reprobate, as to singular persons, has contingently come about from men's antecedent and differing acts. We — if in anything, then especially in this election and preterition — say with the Apostle that God does all things by the counsel of his will (Eph. i. 11).

lemmas.gloss: foresight-scheme snatches election liberty from God
God does all by counsel of his will

title: Cap. X Arg. V open: to be given and not given to Christ is to be ordained or not ordained unto eternal life by predestination and preterition — and that distinction of given/not-given precedes our believing and not believing
latin: Dari et non dari Christo est per praedestinationem et praeteritionem ordinari aut non ordinari in vitam aeternam: At haec datorum et non datorum distinctio antecedit nostrum credere et non credere, perseverare aut non perseverare.
pass_a: To be given and not to be given unto Christ is by predestination and preterition to be ordained or not ordained unto everlasting life: But this discrimination of those given and not given precedes our believing and not believing, persevering or not persevering.
pass_b: To be given to Christ, and not to be given to him, is — by predestination and preterition — to be ordained, or not ordained, unto everlasting life. That distinction between those given and those not given comes before our believing and not believing, before our persevering or failing to persevere.
